subject: ELEC
title: Computer Science Principles
description: A full-year introductory computer science course modeled on the AP Computer Science Principles framework and taught primarily with Code.org's free CSP curriculum. Students study how digital information is represented, how the internet works, event-driven app design, programming with variables, conditionals, lists, loops and procedures, algorithms and efficiency, data analysis and simulation, cybersecurity and cryptography, and the social impacts of computing, with a short bridge to Python. The year ends with an AP-style Create Performance Task and exam review; homeschool students can register for the May AP CSP exam through a local host school. Graded as a college-preparatory elective (UC/CSU 'g'); a UC-approved online provider is needed for a home-designed course to appear on a UC transcript.
framework: California K–12 Computer Science Standards (2018), grades 9–12; CA Computer Science Strategic Implementation Plan; College Board AP Computer Science Principles Course and Exam Description

standards.9-12.CS.1: Describe ways in which abstractions hide the underlying implementation details of computing systems to simplify user experiences.
standards.9-12.CS.2: Compare levels of abstraction and interactions between application software, system software, and hardware.
standards.9-12.CS.3: Develop guidelines that convey systematic troubleshooting strategies that others can use to identify and fix errors.
standards.9-12.NI.4: Describe issues that impact network functionality (e.g., bandwidth, load, latency, topology).
standards.9-12.NI.5: Describe the design characteristics of the internet.
standards.9-12.NI.6: Compare and contrast security measures to address various security threats.
standards.9-12.NI.7: Compare and contrast cryptographic techniques to model the secure transmission of information.
standards.9-12.DA.8: Translate between different representations of data abstractions of real-world phenomena, such as characters, numbers, and images.
standards.9-12.DA.9: Describe tradeoffs associated with how data elements are organized and stored.
standards.9-12.DA.10: Create data visualizations to help others better understand real-world phenomena.
standards.9-12.DA.11: Refine computational models to better represent the relationships among different elements of data collected from a phenomenon or process.
standards.9-12.AP.12: Design algorithms to solve computational problems using a combination of original and existing algorithms.
standards.9-12.AP.13: Create more generalized computational solutions using collections instead of repeatedly using simple variables.
standards.9-12.AP.14: Justify the selection of specific control structures by identifying tradeoffs associated with implementation, readability, and performance.
standards.9-12.AP.15: Iteratively design and develop computational artifacts for practical intent, personal expression, or to address a societal issue by using events to initiate instructions.
standards.9-12.AP.16: Decompose problems into smaller subproblems through systematic analysis, using constructs such as procedures, modules, and/or classes.
standards.9-12.AP.17: Create computational artifacts using modular design.
standards.9-12.AP.18: Systematically design programs for broad audiences by incorporating feedback from users.
standards.9-12.AP.19: Explain the limitations of licenses that restrict use of computational artifacts when using resources such as libraries.
standards.9-12.AP.20: Iteratively evaluate and refine a computational artifact to enhance its performance, reliability, usability, and accessibility.
standards.9-12.AP.21: Design and develop computational artifacts working in team roles using collaborative tools.
standards.9-12.AP.22: Document decisions made during the design process using text, graphics, presentations, and/or demonstrations in the development of complex programs.
standards.9-12.IC.23: Evaluate the ways computing impacts personal, ethical, social, economic, and cultural practices.
standards.9-12.IC.24: Identify impacts of bias and equity deficit on design and implementation of computational artifacts and apply appropriate processes for evaluating issues of bias.
standards.9-12.IC.25: Demonstrate ways a given algorithm applies to problems across disciplines.
standards.9-12.IC.26: Study, discuss, and think critically about the potential impacts and implications of emerging technologies on larger social, economic, and political structures, with evidence from credible sources.
standards.9-12.IC.27: Use collaboration tools and methods to increase connectivity with people of different cultures and careers.
standards.9-12.IC.28: Explain the beneficial and harmful effects that intellectual property laws can have on innovation.
standards.9-12.IC.29: Explain the privacy concerns related to the collection and generation of data through automated processes.
standards.9-12.IC.30: Evaluate the social and economic implications of privacy in the context of safety, law, or ethics.

resources.note: Articles, videos and practice questions aligned to AP CSP

resources.name: CS50x (Harvard)
resources.note: Free lectures and problem sets for the Python bridge and extension

units.title: Digital Information
units.big_idea: Everything a computer stores—numbers, text, images, sound—is an abstraction built from bits.

units.title: The Internet
units.big_idea: The internet works because of open protocols, redundancy and layers of abstraction, not a single central computer.

units.title: Intro to App Design and Programming
units.big_idea: Programs are built iteratively: design for users, write event-driven code, test and debug.

units.title: Variables, Lists, Loops and Traversals
units.big_idea: Collections and iteration let one short program process any amount of data.

units.title: Functions, Libraries and Algorithms
units.big_idea: Abstraction through procedures and libraries manages complexity; algorithms differ in efficiency and some problems cannot be solved.

units.title: Data and Simulation
units.big_idea: Data can reveal patterns and inform decisions, but how it is collected and modeled can introduce bias.

units.title: Cybersecurity and Global Impacts
units.big_idea: Computing innovations create benefits and harms; encryption and safe practices protect people's data.

units.title: Text-Based Programming Bridge (Python)
units.big_idea: The same algorithmic ideas transfer from blocks to a text language like Python.

units.title: Create Performance Task and AP Review
units.big_idea: A well-documented, user-tested program demonstrates mastery of the big ideas of computing.

objectives: Explain how information can be represented with symbols
Define abstraction in computing

days.title: What is computing?
days.work: Set up a Code.org CSP account and journal; list five computing devices you used today and the input, processing and output of each.

days.title: Representing with symbols
days.work: Invent a code using a flashlight (on/off) to send a 4-choice answer to a partner and record how many on/off signals each message needed.

days.title: Abstraction
days.work: Compare a subway map to a real street map and write how each hides details; then describe two abstractions in your phone's interface.

days.title: Bits and patterns
days.work: Calculate how many patterns 1–8 bits can make (2^n) and complete a table showing why 8 bits make 256 values.

days.title: Check
days.work: Take a 10-question check on bits and abstraction and write a paragraph explaining how a touchscreen tap is an abstraction.

objectives: Convert between binary and decimal
Explain overflow and round-off errors

days.title: Binary place value
days.work: Use five flip-cards (16-8-4-2-1) to build numbers 0–31 and convert 10 decimal numbers to binary.

days.title: Conversion practice
days.work: Use the Code.org Binary Odometer widget, then convert 15 numbers between binary and decimal by hand.

days.title: Overflow
days.work: Model a 4-bit odometer rolling over from 1111 and research the Gangnam Style YouTube counter and Y2K overflow examples.

days.title: Round-off
days.work: In a Python or JavaScript console run 0.1 + 0.2 and explain why the result is not exactly 0.3.

days.title: Check
days.work: Complete an AP-style practice set of 8 binary/overflow questions and correct any errors.

objectives: Explain how characters are encoded with ASCII/Unicode
Create pixel images with RGB values

days.title: Encoding text
days.work: Encode your name in ASCII binary and decode a partner's (or parent's) secret message.

days.title: Unicode and emoji
days.work: Look up the Unicode code points for three emoji and explain why ASCII alone was not enough for the world's languages.

days.title: Black-and-white images
days.work: Use the Code.org Pixelation widget to draw a 10×10 black-and-white image and write its bits.

days.title: Color images
days.work: Create a color image using hex RGB values and calculate the file size in bits and bytes at 24 bits per pixel.

days.title: Check
days.work: Quiz on text and image representation; explain how changing bits-per-pixel affects color depth and size.

objectives: Compare lossless and lossy compression
Evaluate tradeoffs of file size and quality

days.title: Why compress?
days.work: Calculate how long an uncompressed 4K video would take to download at 25 Mbps, then discuss why compression matters.

days.title: Lossless compression
days.work: Compress a song lyric with the Code.org Text Compression widget and record your compression ratio.

days.title: Run-length encoding
days.work: Write the run-length encoding for three pixel images and decode one back to the original grid.

days.title: Lossy compression
days.work: Save a photo as JPEG at quality 100, 50 and 10, compare file sizes and visible artifacts, and decide when lossy is acceptable.

days.title: Check
days.work: Write a short comparison of lossless vs. lossy compression for three scenarios (medical scan, streaming video, text document).

weeks.topic: Intellectual property and digital information project
objectives: Explain copyright, Creative Commons and open-source licensing
Apply licenses correctly in a project

days.title: Copyright basics
days.work: Read about copyright and fair use and sort 10 scenarios as likely allowed or not allowed.

days.title: Creative Commons
days.work: Find three images with different Creative Commons licenses and write the correct attribution for each.

days.title: Open source
days.work: Compare MIT, GPL and proprietary software licenses and explain how each could help or hurt innovation.

days.title: Project
days.work: Create a one-page explainer (infographic or slide) on how one type of digital information is represented, using only properly licensed images.

days.title: Unit 1 test
days.work: Take the Unit 1 assessment (AP-style multiple choice) on binary, data representation, compression and intellectual property.

objectives: Describe how devices are addressed on the internet
Explain how data is broken into packets

days.title: What is the internet?
days.work: Watch the Code.org 'How the Internet Works' video on wires, cables and Wi-Fi, then draw your home network.

days.title: IP addresses
days.work: Find your device's IP address and compare IPv4 (32-bit) and IPv6 (128-bit) address spaces mathematically.

days.title: Packets
days.work: Use the Code.org Internet Simulator to send a message split into packets and observe packets arriving out of order.

days.title: Packet reassembly
days.work: Design a packet header with sequence numbers and send a 'postcard' message to a family member split across 6 cards.

days.title: Check
days.work: Answer 8 questions on addressing and packets and explain why messages are split into packets.

objectives: Explain how routers forward packets
Describe how redundancy creates fault tolerance

days.title: Routing
days.work: Run a traceroute (tracert/traceroute) to two websites and map how many hops each path takes.

days.title: Redundancy
days.work: Build a string-and-sticky-note network model and count how many alternative paths exist between two nodes.

days.title: Fault tolerance
days.work: Remove links from your model one at a time and determine which removals disconnect the network.

days.title: Scalability
days.work: Read about how the internet scaled from ARPANET and explain why open, decentralized design helped it grow.

days.title: Check
days.work: Complete AP-style questions on routing and fault tolerance using network diagrams.

weeks.topic: Protocols: TCP, UDP, DNS and HTTP
objectives: Describe the roles of TCP, UDP, DNS and HTTP
Explain issues that affect network performance

days.title: TCP vs. UDP
days.work: Compare TCP and UDP using a video call vs. file download example and list which each would use.

days.title: DNS
days.work: Use nslookup to look up IP addresses for three domains and explain the DNS lookup process as a diagram.

days.title: HTTP and the web
days.work: Open browser developer tools, load a web page, and record the HTTP requests, status codes and load time.

days.title: Bandwidth and latency
days.work: Run an internet speed test at two times of day and explain the difference between bandwidth and latency.

days.title: Check
days.work: Draw the layers of the internet (physical, IP, TCP/UDP, HTTP) for one web page request and take a short quiz.

weeks.topic: The digital divide and internet impacts
objectives: Evaluate the causes and effects of the digital divide
Analyze internet governance

days.title: Digital divide
days.work: Use FCC broadband map data to compare internet access in a rural and an urban California county.

days.title: Effects
days.work: Read an article on how the digital divide affected students during remote learning and summarize three impacts.

days.title: Governance
days.work: Research ICANN and net neutrality and write a pro/con table on net neutrality.

days.title: Global connections
days.work: Use a collaborative document to compare internet access data with a peer or family member from another country or region.

days.title: Unit 2 test
days.work: Take the Unit 2 assessment on internet structure, protocols and impacts.

objectives: Apply a design process to identify user needs
Prototype an app on paper

days.title: Design process
days.work: Learn the design process (empathize, define, prototype, test) and analyze three apps you use for good and bad design.

days.title: User personas
days.work: Interview two family members about a daily problem and write a user persona for each.

days.title: Paper prototype
days.work: Sketch a paper prototype for an app that solves one persona's problem with at least three screens.

days.title: User testing
days.work: Test the paper prototype with a user, record feedback, and revise the design.

days.title: Check
days.work: Submit the prototype and design log documenting feedback and changes.

objectives: Create UI elements in App Lab
Write event handlers

days.title: App Lab tour
days.work: Open Code.org App Lab and use Design Mode to add buttons, labels and images with meaningful IDs.

days.title: Events
days.work: Write onEvent handlers that change screens when buttons are clicked.

days.title: Multi-screen app
days.work: Build a 3-screen app (home, info, quiz) using your paper prototype.

days.title: Debugging events
days.work: Fix five intentionally broken onEvent programs and record each bug type.

days.title: Check
days.work: Submit a working multi-screen app and explain how events control program flow.

objectives: Use variables to store data
Write expressions and string concatenation

days.title: Variables
days.work: Trace assignment statements by hand (a ← 3; b ← a + 2; a ← b) and predict final values.

days.title: Expressions
days.work: Write expressions with arithmetic and the MOD operator and test them in App Lab.

days.title: Strings
days.work: Build a 'Mad Libs' app that concatenates user input into a story.

days.title: Counter app
days.work: Build a clicker counter app that updates a label using a global variable.

days.title: Check
days.work: Complete AP-style pseudocode tracing questions on variables.

weeks.assessment: Tracing quiz and Mad Libs app.

objectives: Use if/else statements
Write compound Boolean expressions

days.title: Booleans
days.work: Evaluate 15 Boolean expressions using comparison and logical operators and build a truth table for AND/OR.

days.title: If-else
days.work: Write a program that gives a different message for a user's age range.

days.title: Nested conditionals
days.work: Build a 'Which Pet Should You Get?' quiz app that uses nested and compound conditionals.

days.title: Flowcharts
days.work: Draw a flowchart for a movie-ticket pricing algorithm (age, day, student ID) before coding it, then implement it and compare code to chart.

days.title: Check
days.work: Complete AP-style questions tracing conditionals in pseudocode.

objectives: Apply systematic debugging strategies
Collaborate in pair programming roles

days.title: Debugging guide
days.work: Write a debugging checklist (read the error, isolate, print/console.log, rubber duck) for others to use.

days.title: Pair programming
days.work: Pair program with a sibling, parent or online partner, switching driver/navigator every 15 minutes, on a decision-maker app.

days.title: Build
days.work: Continue building the app, adding at least two screens, variables and conditionals.

days.title: Test and refine
days.work: Have a user test the app while you silently observe, log every bug or confusion in a table, and fix the top three.

days.title: Unit 3 project
days.work: Submit the app with a short write-up of design decisions and debugging.

objectives: Create and access lists
Use lists to generalize solutions

days.title: Why lists?
days.work: Rewrite a program with five separate variables using one list and explain the benefit.

days.title: List operations
days.work: Practice appendItem, insertItem, removeItem and indexing in App Lab.

days.title: Index tracing
days.work: Trace 10 AP reference-sheet pseudocode problems that use lists with 1-based indexing and compare to App Lab's 0-based indexing.

days.title: List app
days.work: Build a reminder or playlist app that adds and displays items from a list.

days.title: Check
days.work: Complete a list-operations quiz predicting list contents after sequences of APPEND, INSERT and REMOVE.

objectives: Use while and for loops
Choose the appropriate loop structure

days.title: While loops
days.work: Write a while loop that simulates rolling a die until a 6 appears, counting rolls, and run it 20 times to find the average.

days.title: For loops
days.work: Write for loops that count, sum and repeat drawing commands.

days.title: Choosing loops
days.work: Compare while and for for three tasks and justify the choice for readability.

days.title: Infinite loops
days.work: Find and fix the infinite loops in three provided programs and explain the missing update or wrong condition in each.

days.title: Check
days.work: Complete AP-style questions on REPEAT n TIMES and REPEAT UNTIL.

objectives: Traverse a list to process every element
Write filter, map and reduce patterns

days.title: Traversal
days.work: Write a FOR EACH loop and an index-based for loop that each display every item in a list of 10 song titles, then compare readability.

days.title: Filter
days.work: Filter a list of 30 daily high temperatures into a new list of days above 90°F and display the count.

days.title: Map and reduce
days.work: Convert a list of Celsius temperatures to Fahrenheit (map) and find the average (reduce).

days.title: Data library
days.work: Use App Lab's data library to load a real dataset into lists.

days.title: Check
days.work: Solve six traversal problems (count matches, find max, average, filter by length, map to uppercase, find first index) in App Lab.

weeks.topic: Data app project and semester exam
objectives: Build an app that processes real data
Demonstrate semester mastery

days.title: Plan
days.work: Choose a dataset from the App Lab data library and plan an app that filters it based on user input.

days.title: Build
days.work: Build the data app so a dropdown choice filters the dataset with a traversal and displays matching results and a count.

days.title: Test
days.work: Have a user try three different inputs, record any wrong or empty results, and refine the app to handle them.

days.title: Semester review
days.work: Review units 1–4 by completing 30 AP-style practice questions and making a one-page summary sheet of missed concepts.

days.title: Semester exam
days.work: Take the semester exam: 50 AP-style multiple-choice questions covering data, the internet and programming through traversals.

weeks.topic: Procedures with parameters and return values
objectives: Write procedures with parameters
Use return values

days.title: Procedures
days.work: Find repeated code in an earlier app and refactor it into a named procedure, confirming the app behaves identically.

days.title: Parameters
days.work: Write procedures with parameters for drawing shapes of different sizes.

days.title: Return values
days.work: Write functions that return values (tip calculator, letter grade, area of a circle) and use the returned values in expressions.

days.title: Decomposition
days.work: Decompose a game into procedures on a diagram before coding.

days.title: Check
days.work: Complete 10 AP-style questions tracing PROCEDURE calls with parameters and RETURN values.

objectives: Use libraries and documentation
Explain license limitations of libraries

days.title: Libraries
days.work: Read App Lab library documentation and use a library function.

days.title: Create a library
days.work: Write your own library of three functions with documentation.

days.title: Share
days.work: Share your library and use a partner's or a Code.org example library.

days.title: Licensing
days.work: Research the license of a popular open-source library (e.g., p5.js) and explain usage limits.

days.title: Check
days.work: Write a documentation comment (purpose, parameters, return value, example) for each function in your library and take a short quiz.

objectives: Compare linear and binary search
Analyze algorithm efficiency

days.title: Linear search
days.work: Search for a target card in a shuffled deck of 52 cards one at a time, counting steps over five trials.

days.title: Binary search
days.work: Search a sorted deck using binary search and compare the steps.

days.title: Efficiency
days.work: Graph worst-case steps vs. list size (8 to 1,024) for linear and binary search and describe the growth as linear vs. logarithmic.

days.title: Across disciplines
days.work: Show how binary search applies to a dictionary, debugging and guessing games.

days.title: Check
days.work: Complete AP-style questions classifying algorithms as reasonable (polynomial) or unreasonable (exponential) time.

weeks.topic: Unsolvable problems, heuristics and parallel computing
objectives: Identify unreasonable-time and undecidable problems
Compare sequential, parallel and distributed computing

days.title: Traveling salesperson
days.work: Try to find the shortest route through 6 cities and count the possibilities.

days.title: Heuristics
days.work: Use a nearest-neighbor heuristic and compare to the best route.

days.title: Undecidable problems
days.work: Read about Turing's halting problem and write a paragraph explaining in your own words why no program can decide whether every program halts.

days.title: Parallel computing
days.work: Time sorting cards alone vs. with helpers and calculate speedup.

days.title: Check
days.work: Take the Unit 5 assessment on procedures, libraries, search algorithms, efficiency and parallel computing.

objectives: Collect data with a survey
Clean data for analysis

days.title: Data questions
days.work: Write a question to investigate (e.g., teen sleep vs. screen time) and design a 6-question survey with consistent answer formats.

days.title: Collect
days.work: Collect survey responses from at least 15 people using Google Forms and export them to a spreadsheet.

days.title: Clean
days.work: Clean the data by standardizing entries and removing duplicates.

days.title: Storage tradeoffs
days.work: Compare storing data in a spreadsheet vs. a database vs. cloud storage.

days.title: Check
days.work: Submit the cleaned dataset with a reflection on what cleaning decisions you made and how they could affect conclusions.

objectives: Create visualizations that communicate patterns
Choose an appropriate chart type for a question

days.title: Chart types
days.work: Compare bar, line, scatter and histogram charts using four sample datasets and write which question each chart answers best.

days.title: Pivot tables
days.work: Build a pivot table in Google Sheets that summarizes your survey responses by category and counts or averages each group.

days.title: Visualize your data
days.work: Create three different charts from your cleaned survey data, each with a clear title, labeled axes and a one-sentence takeaway.

days.title: Large public data
days.work: Download a CA dataset (e.g., daily temperatures or AQI from a public source) and make a line chart showing a trend over time, noting outliers.

days.title: Check
days.work: Present a 3-slide data story (question, visualization, conclusion and limitations) to a parent and answer two follow-up questions.

weeks.assessment: Data story presentation scored with rubric.

objectives: Build a simulation using random numbers
Refine a model so it better matches real data

days.title: Why simulate?
days.work: Read the Code.org simulations lesson and list three real simulations (weather, traffic, epidemics) and what each simplifies.

days.title: Random numbers
days.work: Write an App Lab program that flips a coin 1,000 times with randomNumber(0,1) and compare the result to the expected 50%.

days.title: Build a model
days.work: Build a checkout-line simulation where customers arrive randomly and one cashier serves them; record the average wait.

days.title: Refine the model
days.work: Time real arrivals at a store or drive-through for 15 minutes, then change your model's arrival rate and add a second cashier to match.

days.title: Check
days.work: Write a paragraph explaining what your model leaves out, how refinement changed its predictions, and one decision it could inform.

weeks.topic: Bias in data and machine learning
objectives: Identify sources of bias in data and algorithms
Propose processes to evaluate and reduce bias

days.title: Bias in data
days.work: Identify the sampling bias in five survey scenarios (e.g., an online-only poll about internet access) and rewrite one to fix it.

days.title: Machine learning
days.work: Train an image classifier in Teachable Machine with deliberately unbalanced training data, then retrain with balanced data and compare accuracy.

days.title: Algorithmic bias
days.work: Read a credible news article on facial recognition or hiring-algorithm bias and identify where in the pipeline the bias entered.

days.title: Crowdsourcing and fixes
days.work: Explore a citizen-science project (e.g., Zooniverse) and write a checklist developers can use to test an app for bias.

days.title: Unit 6 test
days.work: Take the Unit 6 assessment on data collection, visualization, simulation and bias.

objectives: Identify personally identifiable information
Evaluate the tradeoffs of automated data collection

days.title: PII inventory
days.work: List the personally identifiable information you have shared with apps and websites and rate the risk of each item.

days.title: Tracking
days.work: Inspect cookies and site permissions in your browser, then use a tracker-visualizer extension or privacy report to count third-party trackers on a news site.

days.title: Privacy policies
days.work: Read the privacy policy of an app you use and summarize what data it collects, who it shares with, and how to delete it.

days.title: California privacy law
days.work: Learn the rights the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA/CPRA) gives residents and draft a data-deletion request email.

days.title: Check
days.work: Write a 400-word argument on whether location tracking for safety is worth the privacy cost, using evidence from this week.

objectives: Encrypt and decrypt with symmetric ciphers
Explain how public key encryption enables secure communication

days.title: Caesar cipher
days.work: Encrypt a sentence with a Caesar cipher, then crack a partner's message by trying all 25 shifts with the Code.org widget.

days.title: Frequency analysis
days.work: Use the Code.org frequency-analysis widget to crack a random-substitution cipher and explain why letter frequencies leak information.

days.title: Vigenère cipher
days.work: Encrypt with a Vigenère cipher using a keyword and explain why a longer key is harder to crack.

days.title: Public key
days.work: Model public key exchange with the paint-mixing analogy, then explain how HTTPS uses public keys when you load a website.

days.title: Check
days.work: Take a cryptography quiz comparing symmetric and asymmetric encryption and computationally hard problems.

objectives: Identify common cyberattacks
Compare security measures for different threats

days.title: Threat research
days.work: Research phishing, malware, ransomware and DDoS attacks and make a chart of how each works and a real example.

days.title: Spot the phish
days.work: Analyze 10 sample emails and texts, label each as legitimate or phishing, and list the clues.

days.title: Passwords and MFA
days.work: Calculate the number of possible passwords for 8 vs. 16 characters and turn on multifactor authentication for one of your accounts.

days.title: Security measures
days.work: Match firewalls, antivirus, encryption, software updates and backups to the threats they address and note their limits.

days.title: Check
days.work: Write a one-page cybersecurity guide for your family with five specific actions and why each matters.

objectives: Research a computing innovation's beneficial and harmful effects
Use credible sources to support claims

days.title: Choose an innovation
days.work: Pick a computing innovation (generative AI, self-driving cars, facial recognition, ride-sharing apps) and write three research questions.

days.title: Research
days.work: Find at least three credible sources and record evidence on data used, benefits, harms and who is affected.

days.title: Effects analysis
days.work: Build a table of intended vs. unintended and beneficial vs. harmful effects on social, economic and cultural life.

days.title: Write
days.work: Write a 600-word impact essay with citations taking a position on how the innovation should be used or regulated.

days.title: Unit 7 test
days.work: Take the Unit 7 assessment on privacy, cryptography, cybersecurity and impacts.

objectives: Write Python programs with variables, input, conditionals and loops
Compare block-based and text-based syntax

days.title: Hello, Python
days.work: Create a Trinket account, write print statements, and fix three syntax errors in a provided program.

days.title: Variables and input
days.work: Write a Python tip calculator using input(), float() conversion and formatted output.

days.title: Conditionals
days.work: Rewrite your App Lab pet-quiz logic in Python using if/elif/else and compare the two versions side by side.

days.title: Loops
days.work: Write a number-guessing game with a while loop and a times-table printer with a for loop and range().

days.title: Check
days.work: Solve five short Python practice problems (even/odd, FizzBuzz, sum to n, grade letter, countdown) and submit them.

objectives: Use lists and functions in Python
Decompose a problem into functions

days.title: Lists
days.work: Create Python lists, use append, len and slicing, and traverse a list of test scores to find the max and average.

days.title: Functions
days.work: Write functions with parameters and return values (e.g., to_fahrenheit, is_vowel) and test each with three inputs.

days.title: CS50 lecture
days.work: Watch the CS50 Python-week lecture segment on functions and lists and note two ideas that match what you did in App Lab.

days.title: Mini project
days.work: Build a Python program (gradebook, quiz game or word counter) that uses a list, a loop and at least two functions in a separate module.

days.title: Check
days.work: Demonstrate the mini project and explain how your functions decompose the problem.

objectives: Plan a program meeting the AP Create task requirements
Document design decisions

days.title: Requirements
days.work: Read the College Board Create task requirements and make a checklist: input, list, procedure with parameter, sequencing/selection/iteration, output.

days.title: Brainstorm
days.work: Brainstorm five program ideas for a real user and score each on purpose, feasibility and how naturally it uses a list.

days.title: Plan
days.work: Write a program plan with the purpose, the list and what it manages, and the student-developed procedure and its algorithm in pseudocode.

days.title: Prototype
days.work: Sketch the user interface screens and walk a potential user through them to collect feedback.

days.title: Check
days.work: Review the plan against the checklist with a parent and revise any missing requirement.

objectives: Develop the program iteratively
Keep a development log

days.title: Interface
days.work: Build the program's screens and event handlers in App Lab (or Python) and log your progress.

days.title: List
days.work: Code the list that stores your program's data and display it to verify it is populated correctly.

days.title: Procedure
days.work: Write the student-developed procedure with a parameter that uses sequencing, selection and iteration.

days.title: Test
days.work: Write and run at least four test cases, including edge cases, recording expected vs. actual results.

days.title: Peer review
days.work: Share your program with a CS peer through an online community or co-op and give/receive feedback using a collaborative document.

weeks.topic: Create Performance Task: refine and document
objectives: Refine the program using user feedback
Record the video and complete the Personalized Project Reference

days.title: User testing
days.work: Have two users test the program, note usability and accessibility problems, and prioritize fixes.

days.title: Refine
days.work: Fix the top issues, add code comments, and acknowledge any code or media from others with correct license attribution.

days.title: Video
days.work: Record a 1-minute-or-less screen video showing input, program functionality and output.

days.title: Written responses
days.work: Capture your list and procedure code segments in a Personalized Project Reference and practice the written-response prompts about them.

days.title: Submit
days.work: Submit the program code, video and PPR, and self-score with the College Board rubric.

weeks.assessment: Create task self-score with the AP rubric.

objectives: Review all five AP CSP big ideas
Demonstrate mastery on a cumulative exam

days.title: Review: data and networks
days.work: Complete Khan Academy AP CSP practice on binary, compression, the internet and fault tolerance and correct every error.

days.title: Review: programming
days.work: Trace 20 AP reference-sheet pseudocode problems on lists, loops, procedures and Boolean logic.

days.title: Practice exam
days.work: Take a timed 70-question AP-style practice exam under test conditions (120 minutes).

days.title: Error analysis
days.work: Categorize missed practice-exam questions by big idea and redo each with a written explanation.

days.title: Final exam
days.work: Take the cumulative course final and write a short reflection on your growth as a programmer.
